source: Marcello Faletra et al., 2007 Battiato interview (reprinted Artribune, 2021)
evidence_details: Battiato recounts early-1970s musicians recognizing traces of Stockhausen in his work, meeting Stockhausen in Milan and subsequent intensive composition study.
qualification: Strong for educational influence; pre-contact sonic influence was attributed by contemporaries, not explicitly endorsed in identical terms by Battiato.

source: Malte Göbel, taz interview with Franco Battiato (2013)
evidence_details: Battiato dates the later invitation for a project to 1975 and credits it with energizing his study of composition.
qualification: This formal study happened AFTER the Phase01 albums.

source: Roberto Juri Camisasca interviewed by L’Osservatore Romano (2021)
evidence_details: His longtime colleague hears Stockhausen and Cage influences in early Bla Bla albums.
qualification: Period-level attribution, not exact track assignment.

source: Domenico Ruoppolo, OndaRock Franco Battiato monograph
evidence_details: Identifies Clic as dedicated to Stockhausen; associates subsequent experimentation with the composer.
qualification: Critical claim of lessons by 1973 is chronologically questionable given Battiato later dates invitation to 1975.

source: Andrea Bedetti interviews Stefano Pio, GRooVE back Magazine (2026)
evidence_details: Stefano Pio disputes any direct musical influence from Stockhausen, citing diverging views on serialism.
qualification: Conflicts with Camisasca and some professional criticism; never label musical influence undisputed.

source: Roberto Juri Camisasca interviewed by L’Osservatore Romano (2021)
evidence_details: Names Cage and Stockhausen as influences audible in Battiato early Bla Bla works.

source: Domenico Ruoppolo, OndaRock Franco Battiato monograph
evidence_details: Describes two Clic collages as Cage-style.
qualification: A stylistic likeness alone would belong in sounds_like; paired with Camisasca it supports qualified influenced_by for Clic.

evidence_details: Identifies music from Bach Orchestral Suite No. 3 in Meccanica and inspiration for Anafase.
qualification: Borrowed music and explicit musical debt on specific tracks.

evidence_details: Notes Bach fragments included on Fetus.
qualification: Corroborates album-level quotation rather than ongoing global musical influence.

source: Andrea Bedetti interviews Stefano Pio, GRooVE back Magazine (2026)
evidence_details: Attributes Battiato early tape-collage explorations to listening and comparison with MEV and a collective transcribed as M&M.
qualification: MEV originated in Rome, contrary to geographical phrasing in the interview; exact second group identity unresolved.

evidence_details: Describes early Battiato as a Dylan epigone, participating in Bob Dylan-inspired protest singing in 1960s.
qualification: Only pre-Fetus, cannot apply to Phase01 albums.

source: Giuseppe Pollicelli, interview with Franco Battiato (excerpt reproduced 2021)
evidence_details: Battiato credits three years of violin tuition with Pio as foundations of his transition to songs.
qualification: Relevant to post-1975 albums only; article republishes an interview excerpt.
